country.name: Germany
country.tagline: Slate, sugar and the northern edge of ripeness: the country that taught the world what Riesling can do, now making some of Europe's most exciting Pinot Noir.

stats.note: OIV State of the World Wine Sector in 2025 (May 2026). Destatis puts the 2025 must/wine output at 7.55 mhl; the 2026 harvest was estimated at about 8 mhl in October 2026.

country.overview:
Germany sits right on the edge of where wine grapes ripen, and almost everything that makes its wine special flows from that fact. Along the 50th parallel the growing season is long and cool, so grapes hang on the vine into October and November, building flavour slowly while keeping their acidity. Riesling, the grape Germany made famous, thrives on that knife edge: it can give bone-dry wines of lime and slate, featherweight Kabinett with 8 percent alcohol and a lick of sweetness, or Trockenbeerenauslese as thick as honey that will outlive its makers. Germany grows close to half of the world's Riesling, and no other country uses it in so many voices.

The vineyards follow rivers. The Rhine and its tributaries (Mosel, Saar, Ruwer, Nahe, Main, Neckar, Ahr) cut deep valleys into the old rocks of central Europe, and the best sites are the south-facing slopes where the water reflects light and holds warmth. On the Mosel those slopes are made of Devonian slate so steep that vines are tied to single stakes and worked by hand or by winch. In the Pfalz and Rheinhessen the land opens into rolling limestone, loess and sandstone, and in Baden's Kaiserstuhl the vines grow on the terraces of an extinct volcano, in the warmest corner of the country. Thirteen official wine regions (Anbaugebiete) cover about 102,000 hectares, from the Swiss border to Saxony on the Elbe.

History left Germany with a ladder of ripeness. The 1971 wine law ranked quality wine by the sugar in the grapes at harvest: Kabinett, Spätlese, Auslese, Beerenauslese, Trockenbeerenauslese, plus Eiswein from grapes frozen on the vine. The system rewarded ripeness in a country where ripeness was rare, but it also allowed bland, sweet blends to wear prestigious names. The same law merged some 30,000 vineyard names into about 2,600 Einzellagen and invented roughly 160 Großlagen, collective sites that let wine from a dozen villages borrow the name of the most famous one. Cheap Liebfraumilch and Piesporter Michelsberg flooded export markets in the 1970s and 1980s and dragged the country's reputation down with them.

The comeback was led by growers. The VDP, an association of about 200 leading estates, built its own Burgundy-style pyramid (Gutswein, Ortswein, Erste Lage, Grosse Lage) and branded the dry wines from its top sites Grosses Gewächs. The national law followed: the 2021 reform reorganised German wine around origin instead of sugar, demoted the Großlage to a mere 'Region', and made the new rules binding from the 2026 vintage. Germany now sells itself the way Burgundy does, by place.

The other revolution is in the glass. Most German wine drunk at home is now dry (trocken), and warming summers have changed what is possible. Spätburgunder (Pinot Noir) covers more than a tenth of the vineyard, making Germany one of the largest Pinot Noir growers in the world, and the reds of the Ahr, Baden, Franken's red sandstone and the Pfalz now sit comfortably beside good Burgundy. Grauburgunder, Weißburgunder and Chardonnay have spread, Silvaner has been rediscovered in Franken and Rheinhessen, and Sekt made by the traditional method is finally being taken seriously by the growers themselves.

Climate change is a gift with a bill attached. Vintages that would once have failed now ripen every year, but hail, drought, spring frost and torrential rain arrive more often; the July 2021 flood tore through the Ahr valley and destroyed cellars that had stood for centuries. The 2025 harvest came in at about 7.6 million hectolitres, 10 percent under the recent average, and the productive vineyard keeps shrinking slowly as small growers retire. What remains is more ambitious than at any point since the late nineteenth century, when the best Rheingau and Mosel Rieslings cost more than first-growth Bordeaux.

history.title: Romans plant the Mosel
history.text: Roman soldiers and settlers brought the vine to the Rhine and Mosel. Augusta Treverorum (Trier) became an imperial capital in the late empire, and its court and garrisons needed wine. Excavated press houses at Piesport, Brauneberg and Erden show that wine was made on the same slopes that are famous today.

history.title: The Neumagen wine ship
history.text: A stone funerary monument carved around 220 AD shows a galley rowed by oarsmen and loaded with wine casks. Found in 1878 at Neumagen in the walls of a later Roman fort, it is the most famous image of Roman wine trade north of the Alps; the original is in the Rheinisches Landesmuseum in Trier.

history.title: The Speyer bottle
history.text: A glass amphora-bottle found in a Roman grave near Speyer in 1867 still holds liquid: the oldest known bottle of wine, sealed with olive oil and resin. It sits, unopened, in the Historisches Museum der Pfalz.

history.title: Ausonius writes the Mosella
history.text: The Gallo-Roman poet Ausonius described vine-clad slopes reflected in the river in his poem Mosella, the first literary portrait of a German wine landscape.

history.title: Charlemagne's estates
history.text: Charlemagne's gift of the fiscus Hammelburg to the abbey of Fulda in 777 includes the earliest documented vineyards in Franken, and his estate ordinance Capitulare de villis set rules for clean winemaking. Legend credits him with ordering vines on the Johannisberg after seeing the snow melt there first.

history.title: Cistercians found Kloster Eberbach
history.text: Monks from Clairvaux settled in the Rheingau and built one of the largest wine businesses of medieval Europe, with their own ships on the Rhine. They walled the Steinberg, and their cellars still hold historic vintages.

history.title: First written mention of Riesling
history.text: An inventory of the Counts of Katzenelnbogen at Rüsselsheim records money spent on 'riesslingen in die wingarten', the earliest known reference to the grape.

history.title: Schloss Johannisberg goes all Riesling
history.text: After the Prince-Abbot of Fulda acquired the Johannisberg, the estate was replanted around 1720 with Riesling alone, often called the first large single-variety Riesling vineyard.

history.title: The late-harvest courier
history.text: The courier carrying permission to begin the harvest from Fulda to Johannisberg arrived weeks late. The grapes had rotted with botrytis, the wine turned out superb, and the Spätlese (late harvest) was born, at least according to the legend that a statue at the castle commemorates.

history.title: The first Eiswein
history.text: Growers in Dromersheim near Bingen pressed grapes frozen in the hard winter of 1829 to 1830, the first documented German ice wine.

history.title: Maps and crossings
history.text: Prussia's 1868 tax map of the Mosel and Saar ranked vineyards by value, a ranking the VDP later used for its Grosse Lage. In 1872 the Geisenheim research institute opened, and in 1882 Hermann Müller from Thurgau bred the cross that became Müller-Thurgau there.

history.title: The wine law of 1971
history.text: The Prädikat ladder was codified, about 30,000 vineyard names were cut to some 2,600 Einzellagen, and around 160 Großlagen were created. The Nahe became a region in its own right. The law shaped German labels for half a century.

history.title: Origin replaces sugar
history.text: A reform in force from 27 January 2021 reorganised quality wine into an origin pyramid (Anbaugebiet, Region, Ortswein, Lagenwein) and required former Großlagen to carry the word 'Region'. The rules are binding from the 2026 vintage; in 2025 a court refused to let Zell keep 'Zeller Schwarze Katz'.

history.title: The Ahr flood
history.text: A stalled storm turned the little Ahr into a torrent that killed more than 130 people in the valley and wrecked wineries from Altenahr to Bad Neuenahr. Growers rebuilt with help from a nationwide 'Flutwein' campaign.

country.classification:
Two pyramids now coexist on German labels, and a wine nerd needs both.

The legal pyramid starts with Deutscher Wein (no origin beyond Germany) and Landwein (a PGI, 26 regions). Most wine is Qualitätswein or Prädikatswein, which are PDO wines from one of the 13 Anbaugebiete. Under the 2021 reform, origin is layered inside the PDO: the Anbaugebiet (a wine labelled only 'Pfalz' is meant to be dry), the Region (the old Bereich or Großlage, which must now be printed as 'Region Michelsberg' and the like), the Ortswein from a single village (85 percent of grapes from the village), and the Lagenwein from a single vineyard, which must name both village and site ('Hochheimer Hölle'). A Gewann, a lieu-dit within a vineyard, may appear if it is registered. The rule of thumb written into the law is: the smaller the origin, the stricter the rules.

The Prädikat ladder survives as a measure of grape ripeness at harvest: Kabinett, Spätlese, Auslese, Beerenauslese (BA), Trockenbeerenauslese (TBA) and Eiswein. Prädikatswein may not be chaptalised. In practice Kabinett, Spätlese and Auslese increasingly signal fruity sweetness, while dry wines are labelled trocken; 'feinherb' is an unregulated term for off-dry.

The private pyramid belongs to the VDP: Gutswein (estate wine), Ortswein (village), Erste Lage (premier cru) and Grosse Lage (grand cru). Dry wine from a Grosse Lage is a Grosses Gewächs (GG), hand-picked, capped at 50 hl/ha and released no earlier than September of the year after harvest (reds a year later). Since the 2024 vintage the terms Grosses Gewächs and Erstes Gewächs are also defined in the national wine ordinance, and responsibility for classifying vineyards as Erste or Grosse Lage has shifted to the VDP and the national growers' association, so the two pyramids are slowly converging.

Sparkling wine is Sekt; Sekt b.A. comes from a named Anbaugebiet, and Winzersekt is grower-made by the traditional method. Liebfraumilch is a legally defined, mild Qualitätswein from Rheinhessen, Pfalz, Rheingau or Nahe.
country.climate_soils:
Germany is a cool continental to temperate maritime country where every degree of warmth counts. Rivers moderate frost and reflect sunlight; forests on the hilltops (Hunsrück, Taunus, Haardt, Odenwald, Black Forest) shelter the slopes from wind and rain. Most top vineyards face south to south-west at 100 to 350 metres.

The rocks are unusually varied. Devonian slate and quartzite of the Rhenish Massif dominate the Mosel, Saar, Ruwer, Mittelrhein, Ahr and western Rheingau, giving lean, smoky, mineral wines. The Nahe mixes slate with volcanic porphyry, melaphyre and sandstone. Rheinhessen's Roter Hang is red Permian sandstone and shale, while its southern Wonnegau and Franken's Maindreieck sit on limestone. The Pfalz has sandstone, limestone, loess and a basalt outcrop at Forst. Baden runs from granite in the Ortenau to volcanic rock on the Kaiserstuhl and limestone in the Markgräflerland; Franken shows the full Triassic sequence of red sandstone, shell limestone and Keuper marl; Saxony has granite and gneiss on the Elbe.

Warming since the 1980s has advanced harvests by two to three weeks. Must weights that were once exceptional are now routine, which helps reds and dry wines but threatens the delicate, low-alcohol Kabinett style; growers increasingly pick earlier, choose cooler sites and plant fungus-resistant varieties.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.note: About a quarter of the vineyard and the national signature; dominant in the Mosel, Rheingau, Nahe, Mittelrhein and much of the Pfalz. Germany holds close to half the world's Riesling.

grapes.name: Spätburgunder (Pinot Noir)
grapes.note: Second most planted variety and Germany's great red, from the Ahr's slate to the Kaiserstuhl's volcanic soils and Franken's red sandstone.

grapes.name: Müller-Thurgau (Rivaner)
grapes.note: The Geisenheim cross of 1882 that dominated after 1970; still widespread for easy whites, especially in Rheinhessen, Baden and Franken.

grapes.name: Grauburgunder and Weißburgunder
grapes.note: Pinot Gris and Pinot Blanc, both expanding fast, especially in Baden and the Pfalz.

grapes.name: Silvaner
grapes.note: Franken's classic and Rheinhessen's heritage grape; earthy, herbal and deeply food-friendly.

grapes.name: Dornfelder
grapes.note: A deep-coloured 1955 Weinsberg cross that boomed in the 1990s for soft reds.

grapes.name: Lemberger and Trollinger
grapes.note: Blaufränkisch and Schiava, the red pillars of Württemberg.

grapes.name: Frühburgunder
grapes.note: An early-ripening Pinot mutation, a specialty of the Ahr and Franken.

grapes.name: Scheurebe and Kerner
grapes.note: Aromatic crosses: Scheurebe (1916, Alzey) can be thrilling sweet or dry; Kerner was bred at Weinsberg in 1929.

grapes.name: Elbling and Gutedel
grapes.note: Ancient Elbling survives on the Obermosel limestone; Gutedel (Chasselas) is the house wine of the Markgräflerland.

regions.name: Mosel
regions.tagline: Slate cliffs, river loops and Riesling of impossible lightness.
regions.summary:
The Mosel is the most recognisable wine landscape in Germany: a river that coils back on itself between the Hunsrück and Eifel, with vineyards rising from the water's edge at gradients that make farming a mountain sport. It is Germany's oldest wine region and its third largest, with about 8,500 hectares, and Riesling covers more than 5,300 of them. The region includes the tributary valleys of the Saar and Ruwer, which until 2007 shared the official name Mosel-Saar-Ruwer.

Mosel Riesling is famous for doing more with less. Alcohol can be as low as 7.5 or 8 percent in a Kabinett, yet the wines have racy acidity, flavours of green apple, peach and white flowers, and a smoky, stony note that drinkers associate with slate. The residual sweetness in traditional Kabinett, Spätlese and Auslese is balanced by that acidity, which is why a 30-year-old Mosel Spätlese can taste fresher than a five-year-old Chardonnay. Dry wines and Grosses Gewächs have improved dramatically since the 1990s, but the Mosel remains the heartland of fruity-sweet Riesling.

The region divides into the Terrassenmosel (Lower Mosel) from Koblenz to Zell, with its terraced cliffs and the Calmont; the Middle Mosel from Zell to Trier, home to the most famous names (Bernkastel, Wehlen, Graach, Zeltingen, Ürzig, Erden, Brauneberg, Piesport); the Saar and Ruwer near Trier; and the Upper Mosel on limestone along the Luxembourg border, where Elbling and Burgundian grapes grow.
regions.history: Romans planted the slopes to supply Trier, an imperial capital; the poet Ausonius described them around 371, and press houses from the fourth century have been excavated at Piesport, Brauneberg, Erden and Graach. Through the Middle Ages the Archbishop-Electors of Trier and the great abbeys (St. Maximin, St. Matthias, the Carthusians) owned the best land. In 1787 Elector Clemens Wenzeslaus ordered inferior vines replaced with good ones, which in practice meant Riesling. Under Prussian rule after 1815 the region was mapped and taxed; the 1868 Prussian tax map of the Trier district ranked sites in classes that still read like a list of grand crus. Around 1900 the best Mosel wines fetched prices equal to or above first-growth Bordeaux. The twentieth century brought decline: phylloxera, wars, the 1971 Großlagen and a flood of cheap sweet wine. Since the 1990s a generation of growers (Ernst Loosen, Markus Molitor, Clemens Busch, Reinhard Löwenstein, Roman Niewodniczanski at Van Volxem and many others) has restored the old steep sites, and abandoned terraces are being replanted.
regions.terroir: The Mosel cuts through Devonian slate of the Rhenish Massif, 400 million years old. Blue-grey slate dominates the Middle Mosel and Ruwer; the Lower Mosel's harder slate is mixed with quartzite and sandstone; Ürzig and Erden have patches of red Permian (Rotliegend) slate and volcanic material that give spicier wines; the Saar has grey slate with diabase intrusions. Slate warms quickly, stores heat, and drains well, letting vines root deep on slopes that would otherwise be too cool. The river meanders create south-facing amphitheatres (Piesport, Trittenheim, Brauneberg) that trap sunlight, while the Saar and Ruwer, colder and more exposed, give the most nervy, high-acid wines in Germany.
regions.grapes: Riesling (about 62 percent), Müller-Thurgau, Elbling (Upper Mosel), Weißburgunder, Spätburgunder, Kerner, Dornfelder. Red wine has been permitted only since 1987 and remains a small share.
regions.styles: Fruity-sweet Kabinett, Spätlese and Auslese; dry and off-dry (feinherb) Riesling; Grosses Gewächs; botrytised BA and TBA; Eiswein; Elbling Sekt and still Elbling from the Upper Mosel.
regions.classification: Six Bereiche: Burg Cochem, Bernkastel, Obermosel, Moseltor, Saar and Ruwertal. Famous Großlagen (Bernkasteler Kurfürstlay, Piesporter Michelsberg, Zeller Schwarze Katz, Kröver Nacktarsch) must carry the word 'Region' from the 2026 vintage. The VDP's Grosse Lage list draws heavily on the 1868 Prussian classification, and the Grosser Ring auction in Trier each September is one of the price benchmarks of the wine world. Three Uhlen sub-sites at Winningen and Kobern-Gondorf are separate EU PDOs.

regions.name: Saar
regions.tagline: The Mosel's coldest, steeliest tributary, home of Scharzhofberg.
regions.summary: The Saar joins the Mosel at Konz just above Trier, and its last 25 kilometres carry some of the most coveted Riesling vineyards on earth: Scharzhofberg, Bockstein, Rausch, Kupp, Altenberg, Gottesfuß. The valley is cooler and windier than the Middle Mosel, and for much of the twentieth century only three or four vintages a decade ripened properly. In those years the wines were the most electric in Germany: diamond-hard acidity, low alcohol, and a perfume of citrus blossom and wet stone. Climate change has made ripeness reliable, and the Saar has become one of the hottest addresses in German wine, both for traditional sweet Kabinett and Auslese and for dry Riesling.
regions.history: Vineyards were held by Trier's abbeys and the cathedral chapter; the Scharzhof was church property until the French secularised it, and in 1797 Jean-Jacques Koch, ancestor of the Müller family, bought it at auction. In the late nineteenth century Saar Rieslings appeared on the grandest wine lists in Europe. Recent decades have seen a renaissance driven by Egon Müller, Hanno Zilliken, Florian Lauer, Dorothee Zilliken, Van Volxem, von Othegraven and newcomers who have rescued abandoned slopes.
regions.terroir: Grey and blue Devonian slate with intrusions of greenish volcanic diabase (notably at Saarburg's Rausch). Many slopes face south to south-west and rise from the river at steep angles; the valley's exposure to cold air from the Hunsrück lengthens the season and keeps acidity high.
regions.styles: Fruity Kabinett and Spätlese, Auslese with gold capsules, BA, TBA and Eiswein; increasingly dry Riesling and GG.
regions.classification: A Bereich of the Mosel region. The Scharzhof, Ayler Kupp parcels and others carry long-standing reputations reflected in the VDP Grosse Lage list.

regions.name: Ruwer
regions.tagline: A tiny side valley of monastery vineyards and ethereal Riesling.
regions.summary: The Ruwer is a small stream that enters the Mosel just downstream of Trier, and its valley holds only a couple of hundred hectares of vines. It punches far above its size because of two historic monopole estates, Maximin Grünhaus and the Karthäuserhof, and the village of Kasel. Ruwer Rieslings are the most delicate of the Mosel family: very low alcohol, blackcurrant leaf and herbal notes, and a fine-boned acidity that ages for decades.
regions.history: Maximin Grünhaus belonged to the Benedictine abbey of St. Maximin in Trier from 966 until secularisation; the von Schubert family has owned it since 1882. The Karthäuserhof at Eitelsbach was a Carthusian property from 1335. Both estates still bottle wine from the slopes that rise directly behind their buildings.
regions.terroir: Blue Devonian slate on steep south-facing slopes; the Ruwer valley is cool and the wines ripen late.
regions.styles: Fruity and dry Riesling, from featherweight Kabinett to rare Eiswein.
regions.classification: The Ruwertal Bereich of the Mosel region. Grünhaus's Abtsberg, Herrenberg and Bruderberg and the Karthäuserhofberg are monopoles.

regions.name: Rheingau
regions.tagline: A single south-facing slope that became the cradle of fine Riesling.
regions.summary:
Between Wiesbaden and Lorch the Rhine, blocked by the Taunus hills, turns west for about 30 kilometres, and the north bank becomes one long, south-facing slope. That geographical accident made the Rheingau, with about 3,200 hectares, the aristocrat of German wine. Riesling covers about three quarters of the vineyard, and Spätburgunder from Assmannshausen is a historic red island. The style is fuller and rounder than the Mosel, with peach, apricot and a spicy, firm finish, and the region was an early champion of dry Riesling through the Charta association (1983) and its Erstes Gewächs classification (1999).

The landmarks read like a history of Riesling: Kloster Eberbach and the walled Steinberg; Schloss Johannisberg, where the Spätlese was born; Schloss Vollrads, which claims wine sales back to 1211; the Marcobrunn spring at Erbach; Rüdesheim's steep Berg; and Hochheim on the Main, whose wines gave the English the word 'hock' after Queen Victoria visited in 1845.
regions.history: Charlemagne's palace at Ingelheim faced the Rheingau across the Rhine, and the Archbishops of Mainz owned the region for centuries. The Cistercians of Eberbach (1136) organised the vineyards and shipped wine down the river. The first written mention of Riesling (1435) comes from nearby Rüsselsheim, and Schloss Johannisberg's Riesling planting around 1720 and the late-harvest legend of 1775 made the region the reference point for quality. The Geisenheim research institute (1872) trained generations of winemakers and bred grapes. After decades of reliance on big names, the Charta growers (1983) and later the VDP pushed dry, terroir-driven Riesling; today Robert Weil, Georg Breuer, Peter Jakob Kühn, Künstler, Leitz, Spreitzer, Schloss Johannisberg and the state domain at Eberbach lead.
regions.terroir: The slope runs from about 80 to 300 metres. Near the river the soils are loess, sand and marl that give rounder wines; higher up, at Kiedrich, Rauenthal and Rüdesheim, quartzite and slate give tension and minerality. The Taunus forest blocks cold north winds, the broad Rhine reflects light and moderates temperature, and Rüdesheim's Berg, where the river turns north into the gorge, has steep terraces of quartzite and slate. Hochheim, east of Wiesbaden on the Main, is warmer and on deeper soils.
regions.grapes: Riesling (about 76 percent), Spätburgunder (Assmannshausen, Lorch), small amounts of other varieties.
regions.styles: Dry Riesling and Erstes Gewächs/GG, fruity Kabinett and Spätlese, noble sweet BA/TBA, Spätburgunder, Riesling Sekt.
regions.classification: One Bereich, Johannisberg, covering the whole region. The Rheingau defined its own Erstes Gewächs in 1999 and the state's vineyard map ('Gütekarte') of roughly 1,100 hectares underpins the new national use of Grosses and Erstes Gewächs from the 2024 vintage.

regions.name: Nahe
regions.tagline: Germany's geological patchwork, where volcano meets slate.
regions.summary:
The Nahe flows north from the Hunsrück to meet the Rhine at Bingen, and its 4,250 hectares hold more kinds of rock than any other German region. That variety shows in the glass: Rieslings from porphyry (rhyolite) taste smoky and taut, those from slate are lifted and floral, those from sandstone and loess are softer and fruitier. Riesling covers about 1,250 hectares and leads the quality end; Müller-Thurgau, Dornfelder and the Pinots fill the rest.

The Nahe was long treated as a hinterland of Rheinhessen and the Mosel and only became an Anbaugebiet in its own right in 1971. Its reputation rests on a handful of estates: Dönnhoff in Oberhausen, Emrich-Schönleber in Monzingen, Schäfer-Fröhlich in Bockenau, Kruger-Rumpf, Diel and the revived state domain at Niederhausen. The middle Nahe between Bad Münster and Monzingen, with Niederhausen's Hermannshöhle and the old copper mine at Schlossböckelheim, is the heart.
regions.history: The Romans planted vines around Bad Kreuznach. In the early twentieth century the Prussian state cleared rocky slopes at Niederhausen and Schlossböckelheim, using convict labour, to create the Domäne Niederhausen (1902), which made the region's name for decades before falling into decline; it was privatised in 1998 and later revived as Gut Hermannsberg. Helmut Dönnhoff's wines from the 1980s on put the Nahe on the international map.
regions.terroir: The Nahe valley sits on the boundary between the Rhenish slate massif and the Saar-Nahe basin, so slate and quartzite in the north and west meet Permian volcanic rocks (porphyry, melaphyre) and red sandstones in the middle and south. The climate is dry and sunny, sheltered by the Hunsrück; sites like the Hermannshöhle face south over the river.
regions.grapes: Riesling, Müller-Thurgau, Dornfelder, Grauburgunder, Weißburgunder, Silvaner.
regions.styles: Dry and fruity Riesling, GG, noble sweet wines, Pinot whites, Sekt.
regions.classification: One Bereich, Nahetal. Monzinger Niederberg is a separate EU PDO registered in 2018.

regions.name: Rheinhessen
regions.tagline: Germany's largest region, reinvented by a generation of young growers.
regions.summary:
Rheinhessen is a rolling plateau of fields and vineyards inside the Rhine's great bend between Mainz, Bingen and Worms, and with about 27,500 hectares it is the largest wine region in Germany, almost twice the vineyard area of all Switzerland. For decades it stood for volume: Liebfraumilch, Müller-Thurgau and bulk wine. Since the late 1990s it has become the most dynamic region in the country, as growers like Klaus Peter Keller, Philipp Wittmann, Kai Schätzel and the 'Message in a Bottle' generation showed that its limestone and red slate could rival anything on the Rhine.

Two areas carry most of the fame. The Roter Hang between Nackenheim and Nierstein is a steep cliff of red slate and sandstone above the Rhine that gives spicy, mineral Riesling (Pettenthal, Hipping, Ölberg, Brudersberg, Rothenberg). The Wonnegau in the south, around Westhofen and Flörsheim-Dalsheim, sits on limestone and gives powerful, chalky dry Riesling from Morstein, Kirchspiel, Brunnenhäuschen and Hubacker. Rheinhessen also holds the largest share of German Silvaner (about 43 percent of the national total) and Ingelheim's historic red wine.
regions.history: Charlemagne built his palace at Ingelheim, and Worms and Mainz were medieval centres of church wine. The Liebfrauenkirche in Worms is surrounded by the Liebfrauenstift vineyards whose wine gave its name to Liebfraumilch, which by the 1980s was a blended brand of millions of cases from four regions. The 1971 Großlage Niersteiner Gutes Domtal and Liebfraumilch together did great damage to the region's reputation. The comeback began with growers who cut yields, farmed organically and priced their wines against grand cru Burgundy; Keller's G-Max is now one of the most expensive dry white wines in the world.
regions.terroir: A sheltered plateau in the rain shadow of the Hunsrück, Taunus and Donnersberg, one of the driest and warmest parts of Germany. Soils are mostly loess and marl over limestone; the Roter Hang is Rotliegend (Permian red slate and sandstone); the Wonnegau and the area near Bingen add limestone and quartzite (Bingen's Scharlachberg).
regions.grapes: Müller-Thurgau, Riesling (about 5,400 ha), Dornfelder, Silvaner, Grauburgunder, Weißburgunder, Spätburgunder, Portugieser, Scheurebe.
regions.styles: Dry Riesling and GG, Silvaner, Pinot whites, Spätburgunder, fruity Riesling and noble sweet wines, Sekt; plus large volumes of everyday wine.
regions.classification: Three Bereiche: Bingen, Nierstein and Wonnegau. The 'RS' Rheinhessen Silvaner designation was created in 2002 to rebuild Silvaner's image.

regions.name: Pfalz
regions.tagline: Germany's Tuscany: warm, generous, and home to the 'three Bs' of Riesling.
regions.summary:
The Pfalz runs about 85 kilometres north to south along the eastern foot of the Haardt mountains, from Bockenheim to the French border at Schweigen, where it simply continues into Alsace. With about 23,800 hectares it is the second largest region, and the warmest and driest of the classic ones: almonds, figs and even lemons grow in sheltered gardens. Riesling (about 6,000 hectares) gives full, ripe and often dry wines, and red grapes cover nearly a third of the vineyard.

The Mittelhaardt between Kallstadt and Neustadt is the historic core, with the villages of Ungstein, Bad Dürkheim, Wachenheim, Forst, Deidesheim and Ruppertsberg and the great estates Bürklin-Wolf, Bassermann-Jordan and von Buhl (the 'three Bs'). Forst's Kirchenstück, Jesuitengarten, Pechstein and Ungeheuer are among Germany's most famous dry Riesling sites. The Südliche Weinstraße to the south was long a land of cooperatives but now has stars such as Rebholz, Dr. Wehrheim, Becker in Schweigen and Kranz, with excellent Pinot and Riesling from red sandstone and limestone.
regions.history: Roman villas dotted the area, and the Speyer bottle, the oldest bottle of wine in the world, was found here. The region was Bavarian from 1816 to 1945; the Bavarian land-tax survey of 1828 ranked sites by value, with Forst's Kirchenstück at the top. The Deutsche Weinstraße tourist route was created in 1935, with the Deutsches Weintor at Schweigen built in 1936, a Nazi-era project to boost a struggling region. Bad Dürkheim's Riesenfass (1934), a barrel-shaped restaurant, and its Wurstmarkt festival are local institutions.
regions.terroir: The Haardt (northern Palatinate Forest) shields the vineyards from westerly rain, leaving 500 to 600 mm a year. Soils are a mosaic: red sandstone (Buntsandstein) on the hills, limestone at Kallstadt (Saumagen) and Ungstein, basalt from the Pechsteinkopf at Forst, loess and clay on the plain.
regions.grapes: Riesling, Dornfelder, Müller-Thurgau, Spätburgunder, Grauburgunder, Weißburgunder, Portugieser, Chardonnay, Scheurebe, Gewürztraminer, Sankt Laurent.
regions.styles: Dry Riesling and GG, Pinot family whites and reds, Sekt, everyday wines; some outstanding noble sweet wines from Forst and Deidesheim.
regions.classification: Two Bereiche: Mittelhaardt-Deutsche Weinstraße and Südliche Weinstraße. Bürklin-Wolf has used its own Burgundy-style G.C./P.C. labels since the 1990s, inspired by the 1828 Bavarian classification.

regions.name: Baden
regions.tagline: Germany's warm south, from Lake Constance to Tauberfranken, ruled by Pinot.
regions.summary:
Baden is a 400-kilometre ribbon of vineyards along the Upper Rhine and beyond, from the Tauber valley in the north to Lake Constance in the south, with about 15,700 hectares in nine Bereiche. It is the only German region in the EU's warmer wine-growing zone B, and the Burgundian family (Spätburgunder, Grauburgunder, Weißburgunder, Chardonnay) covers about 62 percent of the vineyard. Baden's Pinot Noir in particular now ranks with the best outside Burgundy.

The Kaiserstuhl, an extinct volcano rising from the Rhine plain near Freiburg, is the warmest place in Germany, with volcanic terraces at Ihringen, Achkarren, Oberrotweil and Oberbergen and estates such as Dr. Heger, Salwey, Franz Keller and Bercher. The Ortenau around Durbach grows Riesling (called Klingelberger) and Pinot on granite; the Breisgau, home of Bernhard Huber's estate at Malterdingen, has limestone; the Markgräflerland between Freiburg and Basel is the land of Gutedel (Chasselas). Cooperatives produce most of the wine, led by the Badischer Winzerkeller in Breisach.
regions.history: Romans grew vines here; monasteries such as St. Gallen and Reichenau spread viticulture around Lake Constance. Grand Duke Ludwig of Baden's era promoted quality varieties, and Freiburg's state viticulture institute (founded 1920) bred grapes and later pioneered fungus-resistant varieties. A famous exception allows the Bocksbeutel flask in Baden's Taubertal and in the Neuweier area near Baden-Baden.
regions.terroir: Sheltered between the Black Forest and the Vosges, the Upper Rhine plain is sunny and warm. Soils range from granite and gneiss in the Ortenau to volcanic tuff and loess on the Kaiserstuhl, shell limestone in the Breisgau and Kraichgau, Keuper in the north and glacial moraine at Lake Constance.
regions.grapes: Spätburgunder, Müller-Thurgau, Grauburgunder, Weißburgunder, Riesling, Gutedel, Chardonnay, Silvaner, Auxerrois.
regions.styles: Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris and Pinot Blanc in dry styles, Chardonnay, Gutedel, Riesling, Weißherbst rosé, Sekt.
regions.classification: Nine Bereiche: Tauberfranken, Badische Bergstraße, Kraichgau, Ortenau, Breisgau, Kaiserstuhl, Tuniberg, Markgräflerland and Bodensee.

regions.name: Franken
regions.tagline: Silvaner in a flattened flask, from the shell limestone of the Main.
regions.summary:
Franken follows the zigzag of the Main through northern Bavaria, around Würzburg, Volkach, Iphofen and Klingenberg, with about 6,200 hectares. Its climate is continental, with cold winters and frost risk, and its wines are traditionally dry, earthy and firm. Silvaner (about 1,560 hectares) and Müller-Thurgau dominate, and Franken Silvaner, with its notes of hay, herbs and stone, is the classic partner for asparagus and the local carp. Riesling, Weißburgunder, Bacchus and Scheurebe also grow, and the red sandstone slopes of Churfranken near Bürgstadt and Klingenberg produce some of the finest Spätburgunder in Germany.

Franken's wine comes in the Bocksbeutel, a flattened, round-bellied bottle with EU protection. Würzburg holds three historic institutional estates whose cellars run beneath the baroque city: the Juliusspital (1576), the Bürgerspital (1316) and the Staatlicher Hofkeller under the Residenz.
regions.history: Charlemagne's donation of Hammelburg to Fulda in 777 records the earliest vineyards. Prince-bishops of Würzburg fostered wine for centuries; on 5 April 1659 the first Silvaner was planted at Castell, the earliest record of the grape in Germany. In the 1720s Würzburg's city council ordered its best wines to be filled into sealed Bocksbeutel to fight fraud. Goethe ordered Würzburger Steinwein to Weimar. Bottles of the legendary 1540 Steinwein survived into the twentieth century; Hugh Johnson tasted one in 1961 and found it still alive. Franken's vineyard collapsed after phylloxera and was rebuilt after the Second World War.
regions.terroir: Franken's soils follow the Triassic layers: Buntsandstein (red sandstone) in the west around Miltenberg, Klingenberg and Bürgstadt; Muschelkalk (shell limestone) in the central Maindreieck around Würzburg, Randersacker and Escherndorf; and Keuper marl and gypsum in the Steigerwald around Iphofen, Rödelsee and Castell. The continental climate brings dry, warm summers but severe frosts.
regions.grapes: Silvaner, Müller-Thurgau, Bacchus, Riesling, Domina, Spätburgunder, Weißburgunder, Kerner, Scheurebe.
regions.styles: Mostly dry whites, Silvaner and Riesling GG, Spätburgunder and Frühburgunder from red sandstone, Sekt, some noble sweet Rieslaner and Silvaner.
regions.classification: Traditionally three Bereiche (Mainviereck, Maindreieck, Steigerwald); in recent years Franken has promoted smaller landscape names such as Churfranken and Volkacher Mainschleife. Würzburger Stein-Berg (2020) and Bürgstadter Berg (2017) are separate EU PDOs.

regions.name: Württemberg
regions.tagline: Red-wine country on the Neckar, where Stuttgart has vineyards inside the city.
regions.summary:
Württemberg follows the Neckar and its tributaries (Rems, Enz, Kocher, Jagst) around Stuttgart and Heilbronn, with about 11,400 hectares, two thirds of them red. Trollinger (Schiava) is the everyday local red, pale and light and drunk by the quarter-litre 'Viertele'; Lemberger (Blaufränkisch), Schwarzriesling (Pinot Meunier) and Spätburgunder are the serious ones. Riesling is the leading white. Cooperatives make most of the wine, and much of it never leaves Swabia.

A wave of ambitious estates (Aldinger in Fellbach, Schnaitmann, Dautel in Bönnigheim, Graf Neipperg in Schwaigern, Haidle, Wöhrwag, Fürst Hohenlohe-Oehringen and others) now makes Lemberger and Pinot of real depth. Stuttgart itself has about 400 hectares of vines within its city limits.
regions.history: Vines spread here under monastic and ducal patronage. The Weinsberg viticulture school, founded in 1868, bred Kerner (1929, named after the local poet Justinus Kerner) and Dornfelder (1955). Schillerwein, a rosé-like blend of red and white grapes fermented together, is a regional speciality.
regions.terroir: Steep slopes along the Neckar's meanders, some on terraced Muschelkalk cliffs such as the Hessigheimer Felsengärten, others on colourful Keuper marls. Sheltered by the Black Forest and Swabian Alb, the climate is warm in summer.
regions.grapes: Trollinger, Riesling, Lemberger, Schwarzriesling, Spätburgunder, Müller-Thurgau, Kerner, Samtrot, Dornfelder.
regions.styles: Light and full reds, Schillerwein, dry Riesling, Sekt.
regions.classification: Bereiche include Remstal-Stuttgart, Württembergisch Unterland, Kocher-Jagst-Tauber, Oberer Neckar and the Bodensee areas.

regions.name: Ahr
regions.tagline: A narrow slate canyon making Pinot Noir at the 50th parallel, rebuilt after the 2021 flood.
regions.summary:
The Ahr is a short river flowing east to the Rhine south of Bonn, and its gorge holds only about 530 hectares of vines, almost 80 percent red. Spätburgunder covers about two thirds, giving perfumed, mineral reds that are among the finest in Germany, with Frühburgunder as a speciality. The steep slate slopes at Walporzheim, Dernau, Mayschoß and Altenahr store heat like a radiator, which is why red grapes ripen this far north.

On 14 and 15 July 2021 a cloudburst turned the Ahr into a wall of water that killed more than 130 people in the valley, destroyed bridges, houses and cellars, and swept away barrels and entire vintages. Meyer-Näkel, Jean Stodden, Deutzerhof, Kreuzberg, J.J. Adeneuer and the cooperatives all suffered. Helpers from across Germany shovelled mud, and a 'Flutwein' campaign selling mud-caked bottles raised millions. The vineyards on the slopes mostly survived, and the 2021 to 2024 vintages carry that story.
regions.history: The Mayschoß cooperative, founded in 1868, is Germany's oldest winegrowers' cooperative. Red wine became the Ahr's identity in the nineteenth century, and day-trippers from Cologne and Bonn made the valley a tourist magnet.
regions.terroir: Devonian slate and greywacke on steep, terraced slopes in a narrow valley; the rock absorbs warmth by day and releases it at night. The lower valley around Bad Neuenahr has loess and deeper soils.
regions.styles: Spätburgunder and Frühburgunder reds, Blanc de Noirs, rosé, some Riesling.
regions.classification: Single Bereich Walporzheim/Ahrtal. Top sites: Walporzheimer Kräuterberg, Dernauer Pfarrwingert, Ahrweiler Rosenthal, Recher Herrenberg, Mayschosser Mönchberg.

regions.name: Mittelrhein
regions.tagline: Castles, the Loreley and steep slate Riesling in a UNESCO gorge.
regions.summary: The Mittelrhein follows the Rhine gorge from Bingen to Bonn, the stretch of castles and legends that inspired the Romantic movement. Its 460 hectares are mostly steep slate terraces, two thirds planted with Riesling, and the core lies in the Upper Middle Rhine Valley UNESCO World Heritage Site (2002) between Bingen and Koblenz. The wines are crisp and mineral, somewhere between the Mosel and the Rheingau. Hard work on steep slopes and a shortage of successors have shrunk the vineyard dramatically over the last century, but estates such as Toni Jost in Bacharach, Ratzenberger in Steeg, Matthias Müller and Florian Weingart in Spay and Lanius-Knab in Oberwesel keep the great sites alive: Bacharacher Hahn, Steeger St. Jost, Oberweseler Ölsberg and the Bopparder Hamm in the Rhine's largest loop.
regions.history: Monasteries and Rhine tolls made the gorge rich in the Middle Ages, and its wines shipped downriver to Cologne and the Low Countries. Nineteenth-century Romantic tourism (Turner, Victor Hugo, the Loreley poem of Heinrich Heine) made it famous, but phylloxera and industrialisation emptied the slopes.
regions.terroir: Devonian slate, greywacke and quartzite on terraced slopes of up to 60 percent; the river and rock retain warmth.
regions.styles: Dry and fruity Riesling, Sekt, a little Pinot.

regions.name: Hessische Bergstraße
regions.tagline: Germany's springtime garden on the edge of the Odenwald.
regions.summary: The Hessische Bergstraße is a strip of vineyards along the western edge of the Odenwald between Darmstadt and Heppenheim, about 460 hectares in all. Spring arrives here earlier than almost anywhere in Germany, with almond and cherry blossom in March, and the climate is warm and sheltered. Riesling covers about a third, with Grauburgunder and Spätburgunder behind. The Hessian State Wine Estates run a domain at Bensheim whose monopole Heppenheimer Centgericht is the region's best-known site, alongside the Heppenheimer Steinkopf and Bensheimer Kalkgasse.
regions.history: The Romans built a road (strata montana) along the foot of the hills, which gave the region its name. Monasteries at Lorsch and the Electors of Mainz owned the vineyards; the area became a separate region in 1971 after being split from Baden's Bergstraße.
regions.terroir: Granite and weathered crystalline rocks of the Odenwald with loess on the lower slopes; the hills shelter the vines from east winds.
regions.grapes: Riesling, Grauburgunder, Spätburgunder, Müller-Thurgau, Weißburgunder, Silvaner.
regions.styles: Dry Riesling and Pinot whites, some reds and Sekt.

regions.name: Saale-Unstrut
regions.tagline: Germany's northernmost classic region, on shell-limestone terraces.
regions.summary:
Saale-Unstrut lies around Freyburg and Naumburg in Saxony-Anhalt, along the Saale and Unstrut rivers, at about 51 degrees north. Its roughly 850 hectares (including outposts in Thuringia and at Werder in Brandenburg) are mostly on terraced Muschelkalk slopes, and the wines are dry, fresh and pure: Müller-Thurgau, Weißburgunder, Silvaner, Riesling and the Bacchus cross, plus some Pinot and Portugieser. Low yields after hard winters and tourism mean most wine is drunk locally.

The region holds Rotkäppchen in Freyburg, East Germany's famous Sekt house (founded 1856 as Kloss and Foerster, named Rotkäppchen in 1894), which bought Mumm in 2002 and became Germany's largest sparkling wine company, and the Landesweingut Kloster Pforta, on lands the Cistercians began farming in the twelfth century. At Großjena, a vineyard cliff carries the 'Steinernes Bilderbuch', a series of eighteenth-century reliefs carved into the rock.
regions.history: Viticulture was introduced by monks around a thousand years ago; the Cistercians of Pforta (1137) were key. After 1945 the region lay in East Germany; it became an Anbaugebiet after reunification in 1990.
regions.terroir: Muschelkalk and red sandstone terraces, some loess; a dry continental climate in the rain shadow of the Harz with cold winters and frost risk.
regions.grapes: Müller-Thurgau, Weißburgunder, Silvaner, Riesling, Bacchus, Kerner, Grauburgunder, Spätburgunder, Portugieser.
regions.classification: Three Bereiche: Schloss Neuenburg, Thüringen and Mansfelder Seen.

regions.name: Sachsen
regions.tagline: Baroque palaces and granite terraces on the Elbe around Dresden.
regions.summary: Sachsen is the easternmost wine region of Germany, about 520 hectares along the Elbe between Pirna, Dresden, Radebeul, Meißen and Diesbar-Seußlitz. Vineyards climb steep terraces of granite, gneiss and syenite, often crowned by baroque summer houses built for the Saxon court. The wines are mostly dry: Riesling, Müller-Thurgau, Weißburgunder, Grauburgunder, Traminer and Goldriesling, a local crossing hardly grown anywhere else, plus some Spätburgunder. Schloss Wackerbarth (the state Sekt house), Schloss Proschwitz, Klaus Zimmerling, Martin Schwarz and Vincenz Richter are leading names.
regions.history: Viticulture near Meißen is first recorded in 1161. The Wettin rulers expanded it; Hoflößnitz in Radebeul was their wine estate, and Augustus the Strong's court made Saxon wine a status symbol. Phylloxera arrived in 1887 and devastated the slopes, and in East Germany the region shrank further. It became an Anbaugebiet in 1990.
regions.terroir: Granite, syenite and gneiss weathered on south-facing terraces above the Elbe; the river valley moderates a continental climate with cold winters.
regions.grapes: Müller-Thurgau, Riesling, Weißburgunder, Grauburgunder, Traminer, Goldriesling, Spätburgunder, Kerner.
regions.styles: Dry whites, Sekt, some Pinot Noir.
