de-ahr.name: Ahr
de-ahr.summary: The Ahr PDO is a narrow slate gorge of about 530 hectares in seven municipalities, and one of the most northerly places in the world for serious Pinot Noir. Spätburgunder covers about two thirds of the vineyard and Frühburgunder is a speciality. After the catastrophic flood of July 2021 the growers rebuilt cellars and wineries; production in 2025 rose sharply from the depressed post-flood years.
de-ahr.terroir: Devonian slate and greywacke on steep terraces that store heat in a sheltered valley.
de-ahr.nerd_note: Meyer-Näkel's sisters Meike and Dörte Näkel clung to a tree for hours during the 2021 flood before being rescued, then rebuilt and released the 2021 vintage.

de-baden.name: Baden
de-baden.grapes: Spätburgunder, Müller-Thurgau, Grauburgunder, Weißburgunder, Riesling, Gutedel
de-baden.summary: Baden's PDO covers about 15,700 hectares in roughly 400 municipalities, stretched across nine Bereiche from Tauberfranken to Lake Constance. As the only German region in EU wine zone B, it has slightly different rules on alcohol and enrichment, and it is the home of German Pinot: Spätburgunder is the leading variety and the Burgundian family covers well over half the vineyard. The volcanic Kaiserstuhl, the granite Ortenau and the limestone Breisgau and Markgräflerland each have a distinct style.
de-baden.terroir: Warm Upper Rhine plain between Black Forest and Vosges; granite, volcanic tuff, loess, limestone and moraine.
de-baden.nerd_note: Baden's 'Weißherbst' is a rosé made from a single red variety and stated as such on the label.

de-badische-bergstrasse.name: Badische Bergstraße
de-badische-bergstrasse.summary: The Baden continuation of the Bergstraße south of Heidelberg, around Weinheim, Schriesheim and Wiesloch, with Riesling and Pinot on granite and loess at the foot of the Odenwald; it shares the early spring and almond blossom of its Hessian neighbour.

de-bernkastel.name: Bernkastel
de-bernkastel.summary: Bereich Bernkastel is the Middle Mosel from Zell to Trier-area villages, the heartland of the region's fame: Piesport, Brauneberg, Bernkastel, Graach, Wehlen, Zeltingen, Ürzig and Erden. A wine labelled only with the Bereich name is a blend from anywhere in that stretch; the excitement lies in the single villages and vineyards inside it.
de-bernkastel.terroir: Blue slate in the main river bends, red slate at Ürzig and Erden.
de-bernkastel.nerd_note: The famous Großlage Bernkasteler Kurfürstlay sits inside this Bereich and must now be labelled 'Region Kurfürstlay'.

de-bingen.name: Bingen
de-bingen.summary: The north-western Bereich of Rheinhessen around Bingen, Ingelheim and the Rheinhessische Schweiz. It includes Bingen's quartzite Scharlachberg, Ingelheim's red wine tradition and the porphyry soils of Siefersheim, where Wagner-Stempel works.
de-bingen.nerd_note: Ingelheim calls itself the 'Rotweinstadt', a red-wine tradition dating to Charlemagne's palace.

de-bodensee.name: Bodensee
de-bodensee.summary: Baden's Lake Constance vineyards around Meersburg and Hagnau, at around 400 to 500 metres, benefit from the lake's warmth. Müller-Thurgau and Spätburgunder dominate, including Weißherbst rosé.
de-bodensee.nerd_note: The Meersburg state winery traces its roots to the Prince-Bishops of Konstanz.

de-breisgau.name: Breisgau
de-breisgau.summary: The Breisgau north of Freiburg is limestone and loess country whose star is Malterdingen, where Bernhard Huber (died 2014; now Julian Huber) showed that Muschelkalk can give Pinot Noir of Burgundian finesse. Cistercians from Tennenbach are said to have brought Pinot here.

de-burg-cochem.name: Burg Cochem
de-burg-cochem.summary: Burg Cochem is the Lower Mosel or Terrassenmosel, from Zell to Koblenz, with Bremm's Calmont, Cochem's castle and the terraced cliffs of Winningen and Kobern-Gondorf. Growers like Heymann-Löwenstein and Knebel have shown that its terraces give powerful, dry Rieslings.
de-burg-cochem.terroir: Hard slate, quartzite and sandstone on dry-stone terraces.
de-burg-cochem.nerd_note: The Uhlen at Winningen was split into three separately registered EU PDOs in 2018 according to its soils.

de-burgstadter-berg.name: Bürgstadter Berg
de-burgstadter-berg.summary: An EU PDO registered in 2017 for the red sandstone hillside of Bürgstadt on the lower Main, the first German single-site PDO. Bürgstadt is the home of Rudolf Fürst, whose Centgrafenberg and Hundsrück Spätburgunder are among Germany's greatest reds.
de-burgstadter-berg.terroir: Buntsandstein (red sandstone) on steep south-facing slopes over the Main.
de-burgstadter-berg.nerd_note: The Centgrafenberg is named after the medieval 'Centgraf', a district judge.

de-franken.name: Franken
de-franken.grapes: Silvaner, Müller-Thurgau, Bacchus, Riesling, Domina, Spätburgunder
de-franken.summary: The Franken PDO covers about 6,200 hectares in 141 municipalities along the Main, mostly in Lower Franconia. It is the home of dry Silvaner and the protected Bocksbeutel bottle. The Würzburger Stein, Randersackerer Pfülben, Escherndorfer Lump, Iphöfer Julius-Echter-Berg and Rödelseer Küchenmeister make the region's great whites, while the red sandstone of Bürgstadt and Klingenberg gives some of Germany's finest Spätburgunder from Rudolf Fürst and Benedikt Baltes.
de-franken.terroir: Triassic layers of red sandstone, shell limestone and Keuper; continental climate with frost risk.
de-franken.nerd_note: Franken growers still use the term 'Frankenwein ist Männerwein'; the region's dry tradition is old enough that many wines never bothered with the word trocken.

de-hessische-bergstrasse.name: Hessische Bergstraße
de-hessische-bergstrasse.summary: One of Germany's smallest regions at about 460 hectares in ten municipalities between Darmstadt and Heppenheim. Riesling and Pinot Gris grow on granite and loess along the Odenwald, in a climate so mild that spring blossom arrives weeks before the rest of Germany.
de-hessische-bergstrasse.terroir: Granite and loess on the western edge of the Odenwald.
de-hessische-bergstrasse.nerd_note: The state estate's Heppenheimer Centgericht is a monopole named after a medieval court.

de-johannisberg.name: Johannisberg
de-johannisberg.summary: Bereich Johannisberg is the single district covering the whole Rheingau. A wine with only this name is a regional blend; it should not be confused with Schloss Johannisberg or the village of Johannisberg, both far more specific.
de-johannisberg.nerd_note: Wines labelled 'Bereich Johannisberg' must from the 2026 vintage show the word 'Region' in front of the name.

de-kaiserstuhl.name: Kaiserstuhl
de-kaiserstuhl.summary: The Kaiserstuhl is an extinct volcano about 15 km across that rises from the Rhine plain north-west of Freiburg, and its Bereich is the warmest part of Germany. Terraces of volcanic tuff and deep loess at Ihringen, Achkarren, Oberrotweil, Burkheim and Oberbergen give powerful Spätburgunder, Grauburgunder and Weißburgunder; Ihringen regularly records Germany's highest temperatures.
de-kaiserstuhl.terroir: Volcanic tephrite and tuff overlain in places by loess up to tens of metres deep.
de-kaiserstuhl.nerd_note: Loess terraces were bulldozed into huge flat platforms in the 1970s land consolidation, a scar still visible from the air.

de-kraichgau.name: Kraichgau
de-kraichgau.summary: A hilly loess and Keuper landscape between Heidelberg and Heilbronn, the 'land of a thousand hills', with mixed plantings of Riesling, Pinot and Müller-Thurgau, much of it handled by cooperatives, and a few ambitious estates in villages such as Sulzfeld and Eichtersheim.

de-markgraflerland.name: Markgräflerland
de-markgraflerland.summary: Between Freiburg and Basel, the Markgräflerland is the home of Gutedel (Chasselas), introduced in 1780 by Margrave Karl Friedrich from Vevey. It also makes fine Pinot and Chardonnay on limestone and loess, with stars such as Ziereisen and the Wassmer brothers.
de-markgraflerland.terroir: Loess and limestone, warm and sunny below the Black Forest.
de-markgraflerland.nerd_note: Gutedel is the same grape as Switzerland's Chasselas and covers about a third of the Markgräflerland vineyard.

de-mittelhaardt-deutsche-weinstrasse.name: Mittelhaardt-Deutsche Weinstraße
de-mittelhaardt-deutsche-weinstrasse.summary: The northern Bereich of the Pfalz from Bockenheim to Neustadt, containing the classic Riesling villages of Kallstadt, Ungstein, Bad Dürkheim, Wachenheim, Forst, Deidesheim and Ruppertsberg. This is where the 'three Bs' and Christmann farm their grand crus.
de-mittelhaardt-deutsche-weinstrasse.terroir: Sandstone, limestone, loess and the basalt of Forst.

de-mittelrhein.name: Mittelrhein
de-mittelrhein.summary: The Mittelrhein PDO covers about 460 hectares in 51 municipalities in the Rhine gorge from Bingen to near Bonn, mostly on steep slate. Riesling dominates, giving crisp, mineral wines. Bacharach, Steeg, Oberwesel and Boppard are the key villages, and much of the area lies in the Upper Middle Rhine Valley World Heritage Site.
de-mittelrhein.terroir: Slate and greywacke terraces above the Rhine.
de-mittelrhein.nerd_note: Bacharach takes its name, according to tradition, from Bacchus' altar (Bacchi ara), a rock in the river.

de-monzinger-niederberg.name: Monzinger Niederberg
de-monzinger-niederberg.summary: A small single-site PDO at Monzingen on the upper Nahe, registered by the EU in 2018 for Riesling with a maximum yield of 75 hl/ha. It is one of the handful of German vineyards to seek protection at EU level outside the Anbaugebiet system, a sign of growers wanting to anchor quality to a precise place.
de-monzinger-niederberg.terroir: Slate and weathered volcanic rock on a slope near Monzingen.
de-monzinger-niederberg.nerd_note: Monzingen is better known for the Halenberg and Frühlingsplätzchen, Emrich-Schönleber's two Grosse Lagen.

de-mosel.name: Mosel
de-mosel.grapes: Riesling (about 62%), Müller-Thurgau, Elbling, Weißburgunder, Spätburgunder, Kerner
de-mosel.summary:
The Mosel PDO covers the river from the Luxembourg border to Koblenz plus the Saar and Ruwer valleys: about 8,500 hectares in 131 municipalities, most of them on slopes too steep for machines. It is the benchmark for Riesling at low alcohol and high acidity. A Mosel Kabinett might have 8 percent alcohol and 40 grams of sugar yet taste dry-ish and electric; a Spätlese is richer, an Auslese honeyed, and the region's TBA and Eiswein are among the most expensive sweet wines in the world. Dry Riesling, often labelled trocken or Grosses Gewächs, is now just as important, and grower Sekt from Riesling or Elbling is rising.

The best sites cluster in the Middle Mosel between Trittenheim and Ürzig, at Bernkastel, Graach, Wehlen and Zeltingen, and on the Saar around Wiltingen and Ockfen. Abandoned terraces on the Lower Mosel and side valleys are being replanted by young growers, a sign of a region in revival.
de-mosel.terroir: Devonian slate in blue, grey and red forms, steep south-facing slopes over a river that reflects light and buffers frost.
de-mosel.nerd_note: The Mosel's traditional gold capsule (Goldkapsel) and long gold capsule mark an estate's best Auslese, a private code that predates the 1971 law.
contains: Uhlen Blaufüsser Lay / Uhlen Blaufüßer Lay

de-moseltor.name: Moseltor
de-moseltor.summary: Moseltor is the small Saarland end of the Mosel around Perl and Nennig, opposite Schengen in Luxembourg, where three countries meet. Limestone soils and Pinot varieties link it to Luxembourg and Lorraine.
de-moseltor.nerd_note: A Roman villa at Nennig preserves one of the largest mosaics north of the Alps, a reminder that wine and wealth arrived here early.

de-nahe.name: Nahe
de-nahe.summary: The Nahe PDO covers about 4,250 hectares in 91 municipalities along the Nahe and its side valleys, from Monzingen to Bingen. It is Germany's most geologically varied region, and its best Rieslings combine the Mosel's lift with the Rheingau's body. The middle Nahe holds the stars: Dönnhoff's Hermannshöhle and Brücke, the Kupfergrube and Felsenberg at Schlossböckelheim, Emrich-Schönleber's Halenberg and Frühlingsplätzchen at Monzingen, and Schäfer-Fröhlich's Felseneck at Bockenau.
de-nahe.terroir: Slate, quartzite, porphyry, melaphyre, sandstone and loess in a sunny, dry valley.
de-nahe.nerd_note: The Nahe was split from the Rheinhessen and Mosel orbit only in 1971; before that its wines were often sold under neighbours' names.

de-nahetal.name: Nahetal
de-nahetal.created: After 1971 (merger of Bereiche Kreuznach and Schloss Böckelheim)
de-nahetal.summary: The single Bereich covering the whole Nahe, created when the two older Bereiche (Kreuznach and Schloss Böckelheim) were merged. A wine labelled only Nahetal is a regional blend; from the 2026 vintage it must be printed as 'Region Nahetal', and the region's real interest lies in its villages and single sites.

de-nierstein.name: Nierstein
de-nierstein.summary: The eastern Bereich along the Rhine from Mainz to Worms-north, including Nackenheim, Nierstein and Oppenheim. Its jewel is the Roter Hang, a cliff of red Permian slate and sandstone above the river. The infamous Großlage Niersteiner Gutes Domtal also sits here.
de-nierstein.terroir: Red Rotliegend slate and sandstone on the river cliff; loess inland.
de-nierstein.nerd_note: Oppenheim's Deutsches Weinbaumuseum documents the region's long history.

de-obermosel.name: Obermosel
de-obermosel.summary: The Upper Mosel faces Luxembourg across the river south of Trier and sits on Muschelkalk limestone, not slate. It is the last stronghold of Elbling, one of Europe's oldest varieties, which gives light, tart wines and good Sekt, alongside the Pinot family.
de-obermosel.terroir: Limestone and marl, the same geology as Luxembourg's Moselle.
de-obermosel.nerd_note: Elbling is thought to have been grown on the Mosel since Roman times.

de-ortenau.name: Ortenau
de-ortenau.summary: The Ortenau between Baden-Baden and Offenburg grows Riesling (locally 'Klingelberger') and Spätburgunder on steep granite slopes at Durbach, Neuweier and Oberkirch. Neuweier is one of the few places outside Franken allowed to use the Bocksbeutel.
de-ortenau.terroir: Weathered granite and gneiss of the Black Forest.
de-ortenau.nerd_note: In Durbach Riesling is called Klingelberger after a vineyard at Schloss Staufenberg.

de-pfalz.name: Pfalz
de-pfalz.grapes: Riesling, Dornfelder, Müller-Thurgau, Spätburgunder, Grauburgunder, Weißburgunder
de-pfalz.summary: The Pfalz PDO runs along the Haardt from Bockenheim to Schweigen with about 23,800 hectares in 142 municipalities. It is warm, dry and diverse, making the country's fullest dry Rieslings, fine Pinot, and good everyday reds. The Mittelhaardt's Forst, Deidesheim, Wachenheim, Ungstein and Kallstadt hold the greatest Riesling sites; the Südliche Weinstraße around Birkweiler, Siebeldingen and Schweigen excels with Pinot and Riesling on red sandstone and limestone.
de-pfalz.terroir: Sheltered by the Haardt forest; sandstone, limestone, loess and basalt.
de-pfalz.nerd_note: The region was officially called Rheinpfalz until the 1990s; Bavarian rule (1816 to 1945) left the 1828 land-tax classification that still informs site rankings.

de-rheingau.name: Rheingau
de-rheingau.summary:
The Rheingau PDO covers about 3,200 hectares in eleven municipalities from Flörsheim and Hochheim on the Main to Lorch at the start of the Rhine gorge. It is the most Riesling-dominated region in Germany and the historic home of German fine wine: the place of Kloster Eberbach, Schloss Johannisberg, Schloss Vollrads and the Geisenheim institute. Rheingau Riesling is broader than Mosel Riesling, with peach and citrus fruit, spice and a firm, dry backbone, and the region led the movement back to dry Riesling with the Charta (1983) and its Erstes Gewächs (1999). Spätburgunder from the slate slopes of Assmannshausen is a celebrated red.

The great sites run along the slope: Rüdesheimer Berg Schlossberg and Rottland, Johannisberger Hölle, Winkeler Jesuitengarten, Erbacher Marcobrunn and Siegelsberg, the Steinberg, Kiedricher Gräfenberg, Rauenthaler Baiken and Hochheimer Hölle and Domdechaney.
de-rheingau.terroir: A south-facing slope sheltered by the Taunus with the wide Rhine as a mirror; loess and marl near the river, slate and quartzite higher up.
de-rheingau.nerd_note: The word 'hock' for Rhine wine comes from Hochheim; after Queen Victoria visited in 1845 a vineyard there was renamed Königin-Victoriaberg.

de-rheinhessen.name: Rheinhessen
de-rheinhessen.grapes: Müller-Thurgau, Riesling, Dornfelder, Silvaner, Grauburgunder, Spätburgunder
de-rheinhessen.summary: Germany's largest PDO at about 27,500 hectares in 133 municipalities, Rheinhessen produced over two million hectolitres in 2025 and makes everything from bulk wine to some of the world's most expensive dry Riesling. Its best sites are on the Roter Hang at Nierstein and Nackenheim, the limestone of the Wonnegau around Westhofen and Dalsheim, Bingen's Scharlachberg and the Rheinhessische Schweiz around Siefersheim. Silvaner, Weißburgunder and Spätburgunder are all excellent here.
de-rheinhessen.terroir: A warm, dry plateau; loess and marl over limestone, red Rotliegend slate at the Roter Hang.
de-rheinhessen.nerd_note: Keller's G-Max, from undisclosed old vines in the Wonnegau, has fetched thousands of euros per bottle at auction.

de-ruwertal.name: Ruwertal
de-ruwertal.summary: The Ruwertal Bereich covers the little Ruwer valley east of Trier, with Kasel, Waldrach, Mertesdorf and Eitelsbach. The Rieslings are delicate and herbal, with very low alcohol and long ageing potential. Two monastic estates, Maximin Grünhaus and the Karthäuserhof, own their slopes as monopoles.
de-ruwertal.terroir: Blue Devonian slate on steep south-facing slopes in a cool valley.
de-ruwertal.nerd_note: Karthäuserhof's bottles carry only a neck label and no body label, a tradition dating to the nineteenth century.

de-saale-unstrut.name: Saale-Unstrut
de-saale-unstrut.summary: The Saale-Unstrut PDO covers about 850 hectares in 51 municipalities in Saxony-Anhalt, Thuringia and Brandenburg, around 51 degrees north. Dry whites from shell-limestone terraces dominate, and Freyburg is home to Rotkäppchen-Mumm, Germany's largest sparkling wine company.
de-saale-unstrut.terroir: Muschelkalk and sandstone terraces in a dry continental climate.
de-saale-unstrut.nerd_note: The Werder area near Potsdam in Brandenburg belongs to Saale-Unstrut for legal purposes despite lying 150 km away.

de-saar.name: Saar
de-saar.summary: The Saar Bereich covers the lower Saar valley from Serrig to Konz, with the villages of Saarburg, Ockfen, Ayl, Wiltingen, Kanzem, Wawern and Oberemmel. It is cooler and later-ripening than the Middle Mosel, and its Rieslings have the highest acidity and some of the most precise flavours in Germany. Scharzhofberg is the most famous site; Bockstein, Rausch, Kupp and Altenberg are close behind.
de-saar.terroir: Grey slate and diabase on steep, wind-exposed slopes.
de-saar.nerd_note: Peter Lauer labels its wines by 'Fass' numbers that correspond to historic parcels within the Ayler Kupp.

de-sachsen.name: Sachsen
de-sachsen.grapes: Müller-Thurgau, Riesling, Weißburgunder, Grauburgunder, Traminer, Goldriesling
de-sachsen.summary: Sachsen's PDO covers about 520 hectares along the Elbe from Pirna to Diesbar-Seußlitz in 55 municipalities, the easternmost region in Germany. Granite terraces, baroque estates and dry, aromatic whites define it; Goldriesling is a local curiosity.
de-sachsen.terroir: Granite, syenite and gneiss on south-facing Elbe terraces.
de-sachsen.nerd_note: Goldriesling, a 1893 Alsatian crossing, survives almost only in Saxony.

de-sudliche-weinstrasse.name: Südliche Weinstraße
de-sudliche-weinstrasse.summary: The southern Bereich from Neustadt to the French border. Long a cooperative stronghold, it has become a source of exceptional Pinot Noir, Weißburgunder and Riesling from estates in Birkweiler, Siebeldingen, Leinsweiler, Ilbesheim and Schweigen, some of whose vineyards lie across the border in Alsace.
de-sudliche-weinstrasse.terroir: Red sandstone, Rotliegend, limestone and loess.
de-sudliche-weinstrasse.nerd_note: Friedrich Becker's best Pinot Noir comes from vineyards in Wissembourg, France, which German law lets him label as Pfalz.

de-tauberfranken.name: Tauberfranken
de-tauberfranken.summary: Baden's northernmost Bereich in the Tauber valley around Tauberbischofsheim and Lauda, culturally Franconian, with Muschelkalk slopes, a continental climate, Bocksbeutel bottles and the old red Tauberschwarz grape, which almost vanished before local growers revived it.
de-tauberfranken.nerd_note: Tauberschwarz, nearly extinct by the 1950s, was revived here.

de-tuniberg.name: Tuniberg
de-tuniberg.summary: A small limestone ridge west of Freiburg, next to the Kaiserstuhl, planted mostly with Spätburgunder and Pinot whites and dominated by cooperatives.

de-uhlen-blaufusser-lay.name: Uhlen Blaufüsser Lay / Uhlen Blaufüßer Lay
de-uhlen-blaufusser-lay.summary: One of three EU PDOs carved from the Winninger Uhlen on the Lower Mosel in 2018, at the initiative of Reinhard Löwenstein, who argued that the amphitheatre-shaped Uhlen contains three distinct soils. Blaufüßer Lay is the blue-grey slate section with calcareous inclusions; its Riesling is the most fine-boned and saline of the three. Rules require Riesling, a maximum yield of 70 hl/ha and hand harvesting.
de-uhlen-blaufusser-lay.terroir: Blue-grey Devonian slate with lime-rich fossil layers on terraced cliffs above the Mosel.
de-uhlen-blaufusser-lay.nerd_note: Among the first single-vineyard PDOs in Germany; the name means 'blue-foot slate'.

de-uhlen-laubach.name: Uhlen Laubach
de-uhlen-laubach.summary: The Laubach section of the Winninger Uhlen, registered as an EU PDO in 2018, lies on grey slate rich in fossils. Its Rieslings are broad and smoky, often with more body than Blaufüßer Lay. Like its siblings it requires Riesling, hand harvest and low yields.
de-uhlen-laubach.nerd_note: Löwenstein's three Uhlen bottlings side by side are a textbook lesson in soil and taste.

de-uhlen-roth-lay.name: Uhlen Roth Lay
de-uhlen-roth-lay.summary: Roth Lay, the reddish, iron-rich slate section of the Uhlen straddling Winningen and Kobern-Gondorf, became an EU PDO in 2018. It gives the most powerful, spicy wines of the Uhlen trio.
de-uhlen-roth-lay.nerd_note: The only one of the three Uhlen PDOs whose area extends into Kobern-Gondorf.

de-wonnegau.name: Wonnegau
de-wonnegau.summary: The southern Bereich around Worms, Westhofen, Flörsheim-Dalsheim and Monsheim, whose limestone hills have become the epicentre of modern Rheinhessen. Keller and Wittmann made Morstein, Kirchspiel, Brunnenhäuschen and Hubacker famous.
de-wonnegau.nerd_note: The Liebfrauenstift vineyards around Worms' Liebfrauenkirche lie in this Bereich.

de-wurttemberg.name: Württemberg
de-wurttemberg.summary: Württemberg's PDO covers about 11,400 hectares in 375 municipalities around the Neckar and Stuttgart, and is Germany's red-wine region par excellence, with red grapes on two thirds of the land. Light Trollinger and Schwarzriesling are local staples; Lemberger and Spätburgunder from ambitious estates now rival the best in Germany. The region also covers the Bavarian shore of Lake Constance around Lindau.
de-wurttemberg.terroir: Steep Neckar slopes of Muschelkalk and Keuper marl; warm summers.
de-wurttemberg.nerd_note: Württemberg Schillerwein is a protected Rotling: red and white grapes pressed and fermented together.

de-wurzburger-stein-berg.name: Würzburger Stein-Berg
de-wurzburger-stein-berg.summary: Registered by the EU in 2020, this single-site PDO covers the Würzburger Stein and adjacent Steinberg slopes above the city. The rules are strict: Silvaner, Riesling or Weißburgunder only, 50 hl/ha maximum and dry wines. It turns the most famous vineyard of Franken into a legally protected origin of its own, a model of how German growers are using EU law to fix quality to place.
de-wurzburger-stein-berg.terroir: Shell limestone (Muschelkalk) on a south-facing slope above the Main, with the warmth of the city.
de-wurzburger-stein-berg.nerd_note: Würzburg's Steinwein gave the name 'Stein' to Franconian wine in general in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

sites.name: Bernkasteler Doctor
sites.text: A steep, south-facing slate slope of only about 3.3 hectares directly above the rooftops of Bernkastel, and Germany's most famous vineyard. Legend says Archbishop Boemund of Trier was cured of a fever by its wine in the fourteenth century. A plan under the 1971 law to enlarge the site triggered years of litigation among the owners before its present boundaries were settled. The wines are rich, smoky Rieslings with a mineral bite; Thanisch, Lauerburg and Kesselstatt are owners.

sites.name: Wehlener Sonnenuhr
sites.text: A sweep of blue slate facing south-west across the Mosel from Wehlen, named for the sundial Jodocus Prüm built among the vines in 1842 so pickers could tell the time. Its Rieslings are the archetype of floral, filigree Mosel Spätlese and Auslese, and J.J. Prüm's bottlings age for decades.

sites.name: Graacher Himmelreich
sites.text: 'Kingdom of heaven' rises above Graach between Bernkastel and Wehlen on deep, stony blue slate. Its Rieslings are a touch rounder and more generous than Wehlen's, and Willi Schaefer's Kabinett and Spätlese from here are cult wines.

sites.name: Graacher Josephshöfer
sites.text: A monopole of Reichsgraf von Kesselstatt between Graach's Domprobst and the Wehlener Sonnenuhr, named after the Josephshof estate that once belonged to St. Martin's abbey in Trier. Dense, slate-rich Riesling that needs time.

sites.name: Zeltinger Sonnenuhr
sites.text: Downstream neighbour of the Wehlener Sonnenuhr, with its own sundial in the vines. Deep, weathered slate gives Riesling with a little more power and spice than Wehlen; Selbach-Oster's single-parcel bottlings from ungrafted old vines are benchmarks.

sites.name: Ürziger Würzgarten
sites.text: The 'spice garden' is a near-vertical cliff of red Rotliegend slate and volcanic rock above Ürzig, where vines grow in pockets between rock outcrops. Its Rieslings smell of exotic spice and red fruit, unlike anything else on the Mosel; many vines are ungrafted because phylloxera cannot thrive in the rocky soil.
producers: Joh. Jos. Christoffel Erben (leased to Mönchhof)

sites.name: Erdener Prälat
sites.text: A tiny strip of red slate between rock walls and the river opposite Erden, the warmest microclimate on the Mosel. The 'prelate' gives opulent, tropical Auslese of great intensity. Dr. Loosen's old vines here are a reference.

sites.name: Erdener Treppchen
sites.text: The 'little staircase' takes its name from the steps cut into the rock so growers could reach the vines. Red and blue slate give Riesling that sits between the spice of Ürzig and the elegance of the Middle Mosel.

sites.name: Brauneberger Juffer-Sonnenuhr
sites.text: The heart of the Juffer slope across the river from Brauneberg, with its own sundial. In the nineteenth century Brauneberg wines were among the most expensive on the Mosel, and Fritz Haag's Juffer-Sonnenuhr Auslese remains one of the great sweet wines of Germany.

sites.name: Brauneberger Juffer
sites.text: A broad, steep, south-facing amphitheatre of grey slate opposite Brauneberg. The name is said to come from the unmarried daughters ('Juffern') of a local official who owned vines here. Its Rieslings are firm and slow-ageing.

sites.name: Piesporter Goldtröpfchen
sites.text: A south-facing amphitheatre of blue slate curving behind the village of Piesport, the 'little gold drop' is one of the Mosel's most perfect sites, making juicy, peachy Riesling. Its fame was abused by the vast Großlage Piesporter Michelsberg, which had nothing to do with it.

sites.name: Trittenheimer Apotheke
sites.text: A steep slate slope in the river bend at Trittenheim, the first great site of the Middle Mosel heading downstream from Trier. It gives racy, citrus Riesling with a herbal edge. Coordinates are approximate (Trittenheim bend).

sites.name: Scharzhofberg
sites.text: A single steep, south-facing slope of grey slate in a side valley of the Saar near Wiltingen, about 28 hectares, and arguably the greatest Riesling vineyard in the world. Egon Müller's Scharzhofberger Kabinett tastes of white flowers and lime and lasts for decades; his TBA routinely sets world auction records. Like Schloss Johannisberg, it is so famous that no village name is required.

sites.name: Ockfener Bockstein
sites.text: A steep grey-slate hillside above Ockfen on the Saar. Bockstein Riesling is famous for its cut and its notes of grapefruit and herbs.

sites.name: Saarburger Rausch
sites.text: A south-facing slope above Saarburg whose grey slate is laced with green diabase, a volcanic rock. Hanno and Dorothee Zilliken's Rausch Rieslings, especially their Auslese and Eiswein, are among the most finely etched wines in Germany.

sites.name: Kanzemer Altenberg
sites.text: A long, very steep slope on the Saar's left bank near Kanzem, owned in part by von Othegraven (since 2010 owned by TV presenter Günther Jauch) and Van Volxem. Its wines are powerful by Saar standards, with yellow fruit and spice.

sites.name: Ayler Kupp
sites.text: A rounded hill of slate at Ayl on the Saar. Peter Lauer bottles historic sub-parcels of the Kupp under 'Fass' numbers, revealing how much one slope can vary.

sites.name: Maximin Grünhaus
sites.class: Historic estate with monopoles Abtsberg, Herrenberg, Bruderberg
sites.text: An estate at Mertesdorf on the Ruwer owned by the Benedictine abbey of St. Maximin in Trier from 966 until secularisation, and by the von Schubert family since 1882. The steep slopes behind the manor were divided by their medieval users: Abtsberg for the abbot, Herrenberg for the monks, Bruderberg for the lay brothers. Abtsberg's blue slate gives one of the most delicate Rieslings in Germany.

sites.name: Karthäuserhof
sites.text: The former Carthusian estate at Eitelsbach (Trier), given to the monks in 1335 and secular since 1811. Its monopole Karthäuserhofberg rises behind the buildings, and its bottles famously wear only a neck label.

sites.name: Bremmer Calmont
sites.text: A cliff of slate on the Mosel's outside bend at Bremm, generally billed as the steepest vineyard in Europe, with a via ferrata climbing path through the vines. Romans had a temple on its summit. Kilian Franzen, who took over after his father Ulrich died in an accident in 2010, and a few others keep its tiny terraces planted with Riesling.

sites.name: Winninger Uhlen
sites.class: Einzellage; three sections are EU PDOs since 2018
sites.text: A curved, terraced cliff on the Lower Mosel between Winningen and Kobern-Gondorf, with three soil zones that became separate EU PDOs in 2018: Blaufüßer Lay, Laubach and Roth Lay. Reinhard Löwenstein's dry Rieslings from here are powerful and long.

sites.name: Weingut Egon Müller (Scharzhof)
sites.text: The manor house at the foot of the Scharzhofberg, in the family since Jean-Jacques Koch bought the secularised church estate in 1797. Egon Müller IV makes wines in a traditional style from ungrafted old vines; the family also owns Le Gallais (Wiltinger Braune Kupp) and a Slovak estate at Château Belá.

sites.name: Weingut Dr. Loosen
sites.text: The St. Johannishof estate at Bernkastel-Kues, run by Ernst Loosen since 1988. Holdings in six Grosse Lagen from Bernkastel to Ürzig and a crusading role abroad helped bring Mosel Riesling back to world wine lists.

sites.name: Weingut Joh. Jos. Prüm
sites.text: Founded in 1911 when the Prüm estate at Wehlen was divided, and run by Dr. Manfred Prüm and now his daughter Katharina. Its Sonnenuhr Spätlese and Auslese, often with a reductive, sulphurous youth, are among the longest-lived white wines in the world.

sites.name: St. Nikolaus-Hospital (Cusanusstift)
sites.text: A late-Gothic almshouse at Kues founded by the philosopher-cardinal Nicholas of Cusa for 33 poor men. The foundation still owns vineyards and its cellars house a Mosel wine museum and vinothek.

sites.name: Römische Kelteranlage Piesport
sites.text: The largest excavated Roman wine press house north of the Alps, discovered in 1985 at Piesport-Müstert. Its basins show that wine was made in volume on these slopes in the fourth century, when Trier was an imperial capital. A 'Roman harvest' is re-enacted here.

sites.name: Neumagener Weinschiff
sites.class: Roman funerary monument, c. 220 AD (replica on site)
sites.text: A replica of the famous stone wine ship stands in Neumagen, where the original was excavated in 1878. The carving shows oarsmen and a cargo of casks, and a grinning helmsman who seems to have tasted the load.

sites.name: Rheinisches Landesmuseum Trier
sites.text: Home to the original Neumagen wine ship and a large collection of Roman wine vessels, reliefs and tools from the Mosel valley.

sites.name: Rüdesheimer Berg Schlossberg
sites.text: The steepest part of Rüdesheim's Berg, terraced quartzite and slate around the ruined Ehrenfels castle where the Rhine turns north into the gorge. It gives intense, mineral dry Riesling; Georg Breuer's Schlossberg is a classic.

sites.name: Rüdesheimer Berg Rottland
sites.text: The eastern, slightly gentler part of the Berg, with quartzite and slate under loess, giving fleshier Riesling than the Schlossberg.

sites.name: Schloss Johannisberg
sites.class: Historic estate; Ortsteil site needing no village name
sites.text: A former Benedictine monastery on a hill above the Rhine, acquired by the Prince-Abbots of Fulda, planted entirely with Riesling around 1720 and given to Prince Metternich in 1816. A statue honours the courier whose late return in 1775 created the Spätlese. Its colour-coded capsules (from yellow to gold) mark quality levels.

sites.name: Steinberg
sites.class: Ortsteil site, monopole; VDP Grosse Lage
sites.text: A walled vineyard of about 37 hectares below Kloster Eberbach, laid out by the Cistercians in the twelfth century and enclosed by a wall completed in the eighteenth. Owned by the Hessian State Wine Estates, it gives taut, long-lived Riesling, and needs no village name on the label.

sites.name: Kloster Eberbach
sites.class: Cistercian abbey founded 1136; Hessian State Wine Estates
sites.text: One of the best preserved medieval monasteries in Germany, founded by Bernard of Clairvaux's monks in 1136. Its monks ran a fleet of wine ships and the abbey's 'Cabinet' cellar for reserve wines may have given the word Kabinett. It houses the Hessian State Wine Estates, historic presses, and served as a film set for The Name of the Rose.

sites.name: Erbacher Marcobrunn
sites.text: A low-lying site on deep marl next to the Marcobrunn spring on the border of Erbach and Hattenheim, long the most expensive Rheingau vineyard. Its Rieslings are broad, spicy and long-lived.

sites.name: Hochheimer Hölle
sites.text: A south-facing slope above the Main at Hochheim, the warm eastern outpost of the Rheingau. Heavy marl and limestone give dense, powerful Riesling. Künstler's Hölle GG is a reference.

sites.name: Hochheimer Domdechaney
sites.text: A small vineyard below Hochheim's church, named after the cathedral dean of Mainz who once owned it; deep calcareous soils give rich Riesling.

sites.name: Kiedricher Gräfenberg
sites.text: A steep slope of phyllite slate behind the Gothic village of Kiedrich, high on the Rheingau slope. Robert Weil's Gräfenberg Riesling, dry and sweet, is among Germany's most celebrated, and his TBAs set records.

sites.name: Weingut Robert Weil
sites.text: Founded in 1875 at Kiedrich by Dr. Robert Weil, who had taught German at the Sorbonne until the Franco-Prussian war forced him to leave Paris. Owned by Suntory since 1988 and run by Wilhelm Weil, it is the Rheingau's flagship.

sites.name: Weingut Georg Breuer
sites.text: Rüdesheim estate whose late Bernhard Breuer was a founder of the Charta movement for dry Riesling and left the VDP over classification policy. Now run by his daughter Theresa, it has monopole Rauenthaler Nonnenberg and parcels in Berg Schlossberg.

sites.name: Schloss Vollrads
sites.text: A moated castle near Winkel that documents wine sales back to 1211, among the oldest records of a wine business still operating. Owned for centuries by the Greiffenclau family, it now belongs to a bank foundation.

sites.name: Hochschule Geisenheim
sites.text: The world-famous wine research institute where Hermann Müller bred Müller-Thurgau in 1882, and where generations of German and international winemakers have trained.

sites.name: Rauenthaler Baiken
sites.text: A high site on phyllite and loess at Rauenthal, historically one of the Rheingau's most expensive, giving spicy, firm Riesling.

sites.name: Niederhäuser Hermannshöhle
sites.text: The Nahe's most celebrated vineyard, a steep slope above the river at Niederhausen of grey slate mixed with porphyry and melaphyre. Helmut and Cornelius Dönnhoff's Hermannshöhle Riesling, dry and sweet, ranks with the finest in Germany. Coordinates are near the site's namesake adit.

sites.name: Schlossböckelheimer Kupfergrube
sites.text: A vineyard cut from the spoil of an old copper mine by the Prussian state domain in the early 1900s, with convict labour. Volcanic soils give taut, smoky Riesling. Coordinates are from a trail sign near the site.

sites.name: Monzinger Halenberg
sites.text: A steep slope of blue slate and quartzite at Monzingen on the upper Nahe. Emrich-Schönleber's Halenberg GG is one of Germany's great dry Rieslings, smoky and mineral.

sites.name: Weingut Emrich-Schönleber
sites.text: The Monzingen estate of Werner and now Frank Schönleber, which raised the upper Nahe from obscurity with precise dry and sweet Riesling from the Halenberg and Frühlingsplätzchen.

sites.name: Weingut Dönnhoff
sites.text: The Oberhausen estate whose Helmut Dönnhoff made the Nahe internationally famous; his son Cornelius farms the Hermannshöhle, Brücke (a monopole), Kupfergrube and Dellchen.

sites.name: Niersteiner Pettenthal
sites.text: The steepest part of the Roter Hang, a cliff of red Permian slate rising directly from the Rhine north of Nierstein. Its Rieslings are spicy, concentrated and mineral. Kühling-Gillot, Gunderloch and Schätzel are key owners.

sites.name: Niersteiner Hipping
sites.text: A red-slate slope just north of Nierstein on the Roter Hang facing east over the Rhine, known for vibrant, aromatic Riesling. Keller's Hipping helped revive the area's image.

sites.name: Nackenheimer Rothenberg
sites.text: The northern end of the Roter Hang at Nackenheim, steep red slate overlooking the Rhine and protected as a nature reserve. Gunderloch's Rothenberg has been a benchmark since the 1990s.

sites.name: Westhofener Morstein
sites.text: A limestone and clay slope near Westhofen in the Wonnegau, now among Germany's most famous dry Riesling sites thanks to Keller and Wittmann. Morstein GGs combine power with chalky tension. Coordinates are approximate.

sites.name: Dalsheimer Hubacker
sites.text: A gentle limestone slope at Flörsheim-Dalsheim enclosed by an old wall, and the original source of Keller's fame. Keller's Hubacker GG first showed what the Wonnegau could do.

sites.name: Weingut Keller
sites.text: The Flörsheim-Dalsheim estate of Klaus Peter and Julia Keller, whose G-Max, Abtserde, Morstein and Hubacker dry Rieslings are among the most sought-after white wines in the world. They also make a Mosel Riesling from Piesport.

sites.name: Weingut Wittmann
sites.text: Philipp Wittmann's biodynamic estate in Westhofen, known for limestone-driven GG from Morstein, Brunnenhäuschen, Kirchspiel and Aulerde.

sites.name: Liebfrauenkirche Worms (Liebfrauenstift-Kirchenstück)
sites.class: Church and vineyard; origin of the name Liebfraumilch
sites.text: A Gothic church surrounded by the vineyards of the former Liebfrauenstift. Their wine, 'Liebfrauenmilch', was famous by the eighteenth century; the name was later applied to a blend from four regions that became a global export phenomenon. The Liebfrauenstift-Kirchenstück vineyard itself still exists.

sites.name: Deutsches Weinbaumuseum Oppenheim
sites.text: Germany's national wine-growing museum in Oppenheim, with presses, tools and a collection on the history of German viticulture.

sites.name: Forster Kirchenstück
sites.text: A walled vineyard of under 4 hectares behind Forst's church, ranked at the top of the 1828 Bavarian tax survey. Basalt, limestone and sandstone give Riesling of finesse rather than power; Bürklin-Wolf, Bassermann-Jordan and von Buhl share it.

sites.name: Forster Jesuitengarten
sites.text: Neighbour of the Kirchenstück, once owned by the Jesuits, on sandy loam with basalt. It gives elegant, floral Riesling.

sites.name: Forster Pechstein
sites.text: Named after the black basalt ('pitch stone') quarried from the Pechsteinkopf above Forst and scattered through its soil, the most basalt-rich of the Pfalz's great sites. The dark stones store heat and give smoky, mineral Riesling. Coordinates are approximate, west of the village.

sites.name: Forster Ungeheuer
sites.text: The 'monster' is a larger site south of Forst on basalt and sandstone, giving full, spicy Riesling. Bismarck is said to have pronounced its wine 'ungeheuer gut'.

sites.name: Kallstadter Saumagen
sites.text: A former Roman limestone quarry turned vineyard at Kallstadt, named after its shape (a stuffed pig's stomach, the local dish). Its warm, chalky soils give powerful, long-lived dry Riesling; Koehler-Ruprecht's Saumagen was legendary.

sites.name: Birkweiler Kastanienbusch
sites.text: A high, steep slope on the edge of the Palatinate Forest at Birkweiler, with red Rotliegend slate, sandstone and granite. It gives some of the Pfalz's finest, most mineral dry Riesling.

sites.name: Weingut Dr. Bürklin-Wolf
sites.text: The Wachenheim estate of the Bürklin family, one of the 'three Bs' of the Pfalz and Germany's largest biodynamic private estate. It pioneered Burgundy-style G.C. and P.C. labels in the 1990s, based on the 1828 Bavarian classification.

sites.name: Deutsches Weintor
sites.text: The monumental gate at Schweigen on the French border marking the southern end of the German Wine Route, built in 1936 as a Nazi-era promotion of the struggling region.

sites.name: Dürkheimer Riesenfass
sites.text: A 1.7-million-litre barrel built by a cooper in 1934 at Bad Dürkheim, never filled with wine and now a restaurant beside the Wurstmarkt festival grounds.

sites.name: Historisches Museum der Pfalz (Speyer wine bottle)
sites.class: Holds the oldest known bottle of wine
sites.text: The museum in Speyer displays the Roman bottle of the fourth century found in 1867, still containing liquid wine under a seal of olive oil, plus the Wine Museum of the Pfalz.

sites.name: Achkarrer Schlossberg
sites.text: A steep volcanic hill crowned by a ruined castle above Achkarren on the Kaiserstuhl. Weathered tephrite gives Grauburgunder and Spätburgunder of power and smoky minerality.

sites.name: Ihringer Winklerberg
sites.text: Terraced volcanic slopes at Ihringen, the hottest spot in Germany, protected as a nature reserve for its rare plants and lizards. Dr. Heger's Winklerberg Spätburgunder and Grauburgunder are benchmarks.

sites.name: Oberrotweiler Henkenberg
sites.text: A steep volcanic slope at Oberrotweil on the western Kaiserstuhl, where Salwey makes taut Grauburgunder and Spätburgunder.

sites.name: Weingut Dr. Heger
sites.text: Ihringen estate founded in 1935 by a country doctor, Max Heger; under Joachim Heger and now Rebecca Heger it became the Kaiserstuhl's reference for Pinot.

sites.name: Würzburger Stein
sites.class: Einzellage; VDP Grosse Lage; part of PDO Würzburger Stein-Berg
sites.text: Germany's largest famous single vineyard, about 85 hectares of shell limestone rising above the Main north of Würzburg. 'Steinwein' was the wine of Goethe and of princes; a 1540 vintage was still drinkable in 1961. Juliusspital, Bürgerspital and the Hofkeller share it.

sites.name: Randersackerer Pfülben
sites.text: A steep, south-facing bowl of shell limestone at Randersacker just upstream of Würzburg, giving rich, spicy Silvaner and Riesling.

sites.name: Escherndorfer Lump
sites.text: A steep curve of shell limestone on the Volkach Main loop. Horst Sauer's Lump Silvaner and Riesling, including spectacular TBA, put it on the map.

sites.name: Iphöfer Julius-Echter-Berg
sites.text: A Keuper slope below the Schwanberg at Iphofen in the Steigerwald, named after Prince-Bishop Julius Echter. Gypsum-rich marl gives broad, powerful Silvaner.

sites.name: Bürgstadter Centgrafenberg
sites.class: Einzellage; VDP Grosse Lage; within PDO Bürgstadter Berg
sites.text: A red sandstone slope on the lower Main at Bürgstadt, source of Rudolf Fürst's famous Spätburgunder and Riesling.

sites.name: Juliusspital Würzburg
sites.text: Founded in 1576 by Prince-Bishop Julius Echter as a hospital, still running a hospital, care home and one of Germany's largest wine estates, with vineyards in the Stein, Pfülben, Lump and Julius-Echter-Berg. Its cellars stretch under the baroque building.

sites.name: Bürgerspital zum Heiligen Geist
sites.text: Founded in 1316 by a Würzburg patrician to care for the poor and elderly, funded by wine. Its wine tavern and ancient cellars are a city institution.

sites.name: Staatlicher Hofkeller Würzburg
sites.class: Bavarian state estate, cellars beneath the Residenz
sites.text: The former prince-bishops' wine estate, now owned by the Free State of Bavaria, with its vaulted cellars under the UNESCO-listed Würzburg Residenz.

sites.name: Sommeracher Katzenkopf
sites.text: A shell-limestone slope in the Volkach Main loop, home of the Sommerach cooperative's popular Silvaners.

sites.name: Hessigheimer Felsengärten
sites.text: Dramatic cliffs and dry-stone terraces of Muschelkalk on the Neckar between Hessigheim and Mundelsheim, among the most spectacular vineyard landscapes in Württemberg.

sites.name: Ahrweiler Rosenthal
sites.text: A sheltered slope on slate and loess north of Ahrweiler, giving supple, perfumed Spätburgunder.

sites.name: Walporzheimer Kräuterberg
sites.text: A tiny, terraced amphitheatre of slate at Walporzheim, so hot that wild herbs grow between the vines. One of the Ahr's most famous Pinot sites.

sites.name: Weingut Meyer-Näkel
sites.text: Werner Näkel's Dernau estate, now run by his daughters Meike and Dörte, defined modern Ahr Pinot Noir. Destroyed in the July 2021 flood, it was rebuilt and its Pfarrwingert and Kräuterberg wines are again released.

sites.name: Winzergenossenschaft Mayschoß
sites.text: Founded in 1868 by growers seeking a way out of poverty, the Mayschoß cooperative is generally counted as Germany's oldest winegrowers' cooperative; its cellars were badly hit by the 2021 flood.

sites.name: Bopparder Hamm
sites.class: Einzellage group in the Rhine's largest loop
sites.text: A sweeping slate slope in the biggest loop of the Rhine at Boppard, divided into sites such as Feuerlay, Mandelstein and Ohlenberg, giving lively, mineral Riesling.

sites.name: Heppenheimer Steinkopf
sites.text: A granite and loess slope at Heppenheim, one of the Bergstraße's best Riesling and Pinot sites, close to the state domain's monopole Centgericht.

sites.name: Herzoglicher Weinberg Freyburg
sites.class: Historic terraced vineyard and nature reserve
sites.text: Terraced shell-limestone slopes at Freyburg with small vineyard houses, laid out for the Dukes of Saxe-Weissenfels in the eighteenth century and now a protected landscape.

sites.name: Freyburger Edelacker
sites.text: The best-known vineyard of Freyburg, below the Neuenburg castle on shell limestone; Pawis makes acclaimed dry Riesling and Weißburgunder here.

sites.name: Rotkäppchen Sektkellerei
sites.text: Founded in Freyburg in 1856, renamed after its red-capped bottles in 1894, nationalised in East Germany and bought by its managers after reunification. Rotkäppchen-Mumm is now Germany's largest sparkling wine company; its cathedral-like cask cellar holds a giant 120,000-litre barrel.

sites.name: Landesweingut Kloster Pforta
sites.class: State estate on former Cistercian lands
sites.text: The Saxony-Anhalt state estate near Naumburg, heir to the Cistercian abbey of Pforta (1137), which spread viticulture along the Saale.

sites.name: Schloss Wackerbarth
sites.class: Saxon state winery and Sekt house
sites.text: A baroque palace in Radebeul built for Count Wackerbarth around 1730, now the Saxon state wine and Sekt estate, with terraced vineyards and a belvedere above.

sites.name: Schloss Proschwitz
sites.class: Estate of the Prinz zur Lippe
sites.text: A neoclassical castle north of Meißen, recovered by the Lippe family after reunification and now Saxony's largest private estate.

sites.name: Hoflößnitz
sites.class: Former Wettin wine estate, now a museum
sites.text: The seventeenth-century wine estate of the Saxon electors in Radebeul, with a painted banqueting hall and a museum of Saxon wine history.

sites.name: Meißner Kapitelberg
sites.text: A granite vineyard on the Elbe near Meißen, once owned by the cathedral chapter.

sites.name: Radebeuler Goldener Wagen
sites.text: A steep terraced slope below the Spitzhaus in Radebeul, one of Saxony's most famous sites.

sites.name: Pillnitzer Königlicher Weinberg
sites.text: The royal vineyard below the Pillnitz palace on the Elbe, planted for the Saxon kings.

sites.name: Maximin Grünhäuser Abtsberg
sites.text: The steep blue-slate slope rising directly behind the Grünhaus manor at Mertesdorf, once reserved for the abbot of St. Maximin. Its Rieslings are the most refined of the estate's three sites, floral and long-lived. Coordinates are on the slope above the manor (approximate).

sites.name: Eitelsbacher Karthäuserhofberg
sites.text: The Karthäuserhof's monopole, a south-facing slate slope above the estate at Eitelsbach, worked by the Carthusians from 1335. It gives racy, herbal Ruwer Riesling. Coordinates approximate.

sites.name: Wiltinger Braune Kupp
sites.text: A slate slope at Wiltingen owned as a monopole by the Le Gallais estate, run by Egon Müller since 1954; it gives slightly broader Riesling than the Scharzhofberg. Coordinates mark Wiltingen and are approximate.

sites.name: Trier (Augusta Treverorum)
sites.text: The Porta Nigra and the Roman monuments of Trier, a capital of the late empire, are the reason vines were planted on the Mosel: the court, the army and the city drank its wine. The city's charitable foundations and the Bischöfliche Weingüter still own famous vineyards.

sites.name: Kessler Sekt, Esslingen
sites.text: Georg Christian Kessler, who had worked for Veuve Clicquot in Reims, founded his sparkling-wine house in Esslingen am Neckar in 1826, making it the oldest Sekt producer in Germany. Coordinates mark Esslingen's old town (approximate).

sites.name: Henkell, Wiesbaden
sites.text: Founded in Mainz in 1832 and based in its palatial Biebrich headquarters in Wiesbaden since 1909, Henkell is now part of Henkell Freixenet, the world's largest sparkling-wine group. Coordinates approximate.

sites.name: Loreley
sites.text: The slate rock above the narrowest bend of the Rhine at St. Goarshausen, the heart of the Upper Middle Rhine Valley World Heritage Site and of German Romantic legend, with steep vineyards on both banks.

sites.name: Kaiserstuhl
sites.text: The volcanic massif rising from the Rhine plain near Freiburg, the warmest place in Germany and the heart of Baden Pinot. Its terraces and loess gullies are a protected landscape.
